confidence_scope: Partial engagement is established in read texts; no accessible source located that derives assessment-sensitive retrospective retraction from worldly-information safety. Access gaps and incomplete reference indexing prevent a literature-wide absence or novelty claim.
addressed_criterion: A read account explicitly relates worldly-information safety for modal knowledge to the truth of the same earlier utterance under a changed assessment context and its retraction obligation.
partial_basis: Mighty Knowledge itself combines a retraction motivation, assessor-based rejection, a worldly-information safety semantics, and an optional assessor-credence interpretation. Dinges2021 directly links safety-type estimates with retraction behavior while rejecting the need for relativism. Neither supplies the exact requested integration.

query_receipts.query: A Probabilistic Approach to Epistemic Safety from the Perspective of Ascribers

evidence.claim: Retraction is explained as no longer standing by the update associated with an earlier modal assertion; this is a motivational story, not the formal fixed-use assessment rule.
A modal-knowledge ascription is rejected using assessor information; explicitly cites MacFarlane2014. The OpenAlex reference list missed that citation.
Knowledge combines truth, belief and worldly-information safety across nearby worlds. The safety condition is separately stated from truth at an information index.

Worldly information may be contextually selected; contextual probability may model a conversational participant’s or assessor’s provisionally revised credences. Utterance-context selection and assessment-sensitive retraction are not identified or derived here.

Retraction evaluates an earlier assertion with its use context fixed and its assessment context changed. The2011 chapter applies this to epistemic modals. Rejection permission is not identical to retraction obligation.

Explains retraction of knowledge ascriptions through stakes-dependent estimates of epistemic qualities, extendable to safety/reliability; offered consistently with denying relativism. It is a rival behavioral bridge, not the requested worldly-information semantics.
Cites Beddor–Goldstein on modal knowledge but leaves truth/correctness/agreement/retraction pragmatics to further development, compatible with multiple approaches.
Abstract explicitly advertises safety-semantics comparison in appendices; full text not retrieved, so no conclusion about its treatment of retraction.
Co-cites Mighty Knowledge and MacFarlane2011; gives stable acceptance semantics. Neither the abstract nor its citation link verifies the specific L3 relation.
Reports support for some truth-value shifts but weak average support for the retraction norm. Full text unavailable; a live empirical qualification, not a settled refutation.

Ascriber-relative probabilistic safety is explicitly proposed. Ascriber-relative evaluation is not automatically assessment-relative truth for an earlier utterance; full-text retraction treatment unverified.

findings.finding: L3 is partially engaged; the exact safety-to-retraction derivation was not located.
The existing safety anchor already discusses retraction and assessor-dependent information.
OpenAlex omitted an actual MacFarlane2014 citation; citation absence is unreliable.
Dinges connects safety-type estimates to retraction while denying relativism.
Holliday–Mandelkern leaves the relevant retraction pragmatics underdeveloped.
Hawke2024 comparisons and current empirical work remain inaccessible; no novelty certification.

coverage: The original bibliography contains 53 works from 1967–2024, only four from 2020 onward and none after 2024. The prior 26 available PDFs cover 1996–2024, with most dated 1996–2021; three are from 2020 onward. The October 28, 2026 sweep searched 2018–2026 literature on contextualism, relativism, expressivism, dynamic semantics, epistemic contradictions, probability operators, retraction and assessment sensitivity. Across the initial sweep and focused L3 followup, 44 modern candidates were recorded and 25 exact full texts obtained, plus three previously missing originals; 54 PDFs are now local in total (26 pre-existing and 28 additions). Coverage includes recent surveys, formal models, empirical tests and responses, but 19 selected modern works and 24 originals remain unavailable to this client (43 operator requests). Older foundational chapters, complete books, the strongest 2024 safety/expressivism comparisons and recent empirical reviews remain material access gaps. This is a ranked, bounded search of indexes and public sources, not an exhaustive review. A failed search or inaccessible paper does not establish an open problem or novelty. The old lack-of-model/test claim is addressed; the other two flagged problems are partially addressed. Acquired files have not been extracted into the frozen ARA evidence: existing route verdicts and generated arguments therefore retain their original evidential limits. The focused L3 verdict is partial: Beddor–Goldstein already engages retraction and assessor information, and Dinges (2021) explains retraction through estimates of epistemic qualities, including safety. The accessible texts do not establish a derivation of MacFarlane’s assessment-sensitive retraction obligation from worldly-information safety. The two strongest Hawke (2024) comparisons remain inaccessible; no novelty claim follows.
